CHILD TAX CREDIT CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What's your Child Tax Credit worth?

The federal Child Tax Credit is $2,200 per qualifying child under 17 with a Social Security number, plus $500 per other dependent (an ITIN-only child, a dependent who turned 17, or a qualifying relative) — made permanent by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act starting tax year 2025. Both shrink together once modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) clears $200,000 (single/HoH/QSS/MFS) or $400,000 (joint), and up to $1,700 per child can come back as a refund even if you owe no tax. This applies the phase-out, the filer-SSN requirement, and the refundable-ceiling formula.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing status, income & eligibility

Earned income is wages and self-employment income only — not investment income, Social Security, or unemployment benefits. It is used only for the refundable Additional Child Tax Credit ceiling below.

2. Dependents

A dependent counts as a "qualifying child" only with a Social Security number valid for employment and under age 17 by December 31 — otherwise count them as an "other dependent" for the $500 Credit for Other Dependents instead.

Fill in filing status, MAGI, earned income, the SSN checkbox, and your dependents, then click Calculate.

Estimate

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This estimates these two credits only — not your total tax liability, other deductions or credits, or state tax.
  • The refundable ceiling is a maximum, not a guaranteed refund. It does not model total tax liability, so it cannot say how much of the Child Tax Credit is used nonrefundably first.
  • Ages, SSNs, and relationships are self-reported — this tool does not verify any of them.
  • Federal only. Most states offer their own, separate child tax credit or none at all — check your state.

Common questions

How much is the Child Tax Credit?

$2,200 per qualifying child under age 17 (by December 31) with a Social Security number valid for employment. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act made this amount permanent starting tax year 2025, with inflation indexing going forward -- it is still $2,200 for 2026.

What if my dependent doesn't have a Social Security number?

A dependent with only an ITIN instead of an SSN, or a dependent who turned 17 during the year, does not qualify for the Child Tax Credit -- but may qualify for the separate $500 Credit for Other Dependents (ODC) instead. The ODC is entirely nonrefundable, unlike the Child Tax Credit's refundable Additional Child Tax Credit portion.

Do I need a Social Security number myself to claim these credits?

Yes -- an OBBBA change. The taxpayer (and, on a joint return, at least one spouse) must have a Social Security number valid for employment to claim either the Child Tax Credit or the Credit for Other Dependents, even if the child has a valid SSN. A couple where both spouses hold only an ITIN cannot claim either credit.

What is the income phase-out?

The combined Child Tax Credit and Credit for Other Dependents is reduced $50 for every $1,000, or part of $1,000, that modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $200,000 (single, head of household, qualifying surviving spouse, or married filing separately) or $400,000 (married filing jointly). Even $1 over the threshold costs a full $50 -- the reduction rounds up to the next $1,000.

What is the refundable Additional Child Tax Credit?

Up to $1,700 per qualifying child of an unused Child Tax Credit can be refunded even if you owe no tax, called the Additional Child Tax Credit (ACTC). It is capped at the smallest of $1,700 per qualifying child, 15% of your earned income over $2,500, and the Child Tax Credit remaining after the phase-out. This calculator reports that ceiling, not a guaranteed refund -- the actual amount also depends on your total tax liability, which this tool does not model. The Credit for Other Dependents is never refundable.

Can I claim this if I file married filing separately?

Yes. Unlike this portfolio's own senior-deduction-calculator, which excludes married filing separately entirely, MFS filers can claim the Child Tax Credit and Credit for Other Dependents for the dependents they support, using the same $200,000 phase-out threshold a single filer uses.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published statutory amounts, phase-out formula, and eligibility rules to the numbers and checkboxes you enter. It is not a full tax return, does not model your total tax liability, does not verify Social Security numbers or ages, and is not a substitute for reviewing the IRS's own guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own dependents' ages, Social Security number status, and MAGI before filing. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also checking a new car loan deduction or the new senior deduction? See the auto loan interest deduction calculator and the senior deduction calculator (that one excludes married filing separately entirely — the opposite of this one). Opening a Trump Account for a child born 2025-2028? See the Trump Account calculator — a separate, stackable federal child savings provision from this credit.

Working, with a lower income? See the EITC calculator — a separate federal credit built on earned income rather than a per-child amount, and often claimed alongside this one on the same return.

Estimating this by hand instead? See where a hand calculation of this credit usually goes wrong.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. working out the Child Tax Credit by hand

The headline number — $2,200 per child — is easy to remember. The part that goes wrong by hand is everything downstream of it: the smaller credit for dependents who do not qualify, the rounding rule on the phase-out, and what the refundable portion actually promises.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Dependents without an SSNAssumes a dependent with only an ITIN, or who turned 17, gets nothing.Applies the separate $500 Credit for Other Dependents to them automatically.
Phase-out roundingUses a smooth percentage instead of the stepped rule, understating the reduction just above each $1,000 line.Rounds UP to the next $1,000 of MAGI over the threshold, exactly as the statute's "or fraction thereof" language requires.
Which pool the phase-out hitsSplits the reduction evenly, or guesses, between the CTC and ODC amounts.Applies the reduction to the ODC pool first, then spills any remainder into the CTC pool -- the same split the IRS's own worksheet produces.
The refundable ceilingReports the ACTC ceiling as "your refund."Labels it a maximum, and explains that the real refund also depends on tax liability this tool does not model.
Filer's own SSNAssumes the credit is available because the CHILD has a valid SSN.Checks the filer's own SSN status first and zeroes the credit with an explanation if it is missing.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Forgetting the $500 Credit for Other Dependents entirely -- treating a dependent who has only an ITIN, or who turned 17 during the year, as simply not counting for anything. They usually still qualify for the separate, smaller, entirely nonrefundable $500 credit.

What's the second most common mistake?

Getting the phase-out rounding wrong. The reduction is $50 for every $1,000 OR PART OF $1,000 of MAGI over the threshold -- so $1 over the line costs the same full $50 as $999 over it. A hand estimate that uses a continuous percentage instead of this stepped, round-up rule understates the reduction just above each $1,000 boundary.

What arithmetic mistake gets made most often?

Treating the refundable Additional Child Tax Credit ceiling as a guaranteed refund rather than a maximum. The actual refund depends on how much of the credit is needed to offset tax liability first -- a hand estimate that reports the ceiling as "your refund" can overstate what actually comes back.

What eligibility mistake gets made most often?

Missing the OBBBA filer Social Security number requirement -- assuming that because the CHILD has a valid SSN, the credit is automatically available. The taxpayer (and, on a joint return, at least one spouse) must also have a valid SSN, or neither credit can be claimed at all.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page computes your total tax liability or models any credit or deduction besides these two. Both apply the same published federal credit and phase-out rules to the numbers you enter; verify against IRS guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply published federal Child Tax Credit rules to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.
